root.meaning: sandy harbour, trading place on the sand
root.note: A place name: sand + wīc ‘trading town, harbour’ (wīc was borrowed early from Latin vīcus ‘village’). The food is named after the Earl of Sandwich, whose title came from the town.

stages.meaning: a noble title named after the town
meat between two slices of bread

history: The sandwich is named after a person, and the person is named after a town. John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, lived in the 1700s. A French visitor to London wrote that the Earl once played cards for 24 hours and ate only beef between two pieces of toast, so he did not have to stop. Others think he ate this way while he worked at his desk. People started to ask for ‘the same as Sandwich’, and the word is in print by 1762. The town of Sandwich in Kent is much older. In Old English, Sandwīc meant ‘sandy harbour’ or ‘trading place on the sand’. People ate bread with things in it long before the Earl, of course, but he gave the food its name.
historyEinfach: The sandwich has its name from a man: the Earl of Sandwich. He lived in England about 250 years ago. The story says that he played cards all day and all night. He did not want to stop, so he ate meat between two pieces of bread. Sandwich is also a small town in England. It is very old.

synonyms.note: northern England, informal: a chip butty
a sandwich made with a small round bread

chain: Japanese サンドイッチ sandoitchi
elsewhere.text: Japanese borrowed the word and then cut it to sando, as in katsu sando, a sandwich with fried pork. Japanese often shortens long English loanwords like this.
